problem: There is no fast, scalable way to measure how human-like an agent's navigation is. Human Turing Tests are accurate but costly, rule-based detectors (e.g., 'getting stuck') are coarse and need expert effort, and navigation research mostly evaluates task success only.
motivation: Learning human-like behavior needs a cheap proxy for human judgment that could drive agent development at scale. The authors observe that state-of-the-art RL navigation agents reach high task success yet are still easily told apart from humans. So success is not sufficient, and a learned discriminator validated against real human judges is needed.
key_idea: Train classifiers to tell human from agent navigation trajectories, using only the known trajectory source as proxy labels. Then validate these automated judges (ANTT) against ground-truth human Turing Test judgments (HNTT) collected only on held-out test videos.
insight: The input representation matters, but not the way one would expect. Symbolic classifiers on 3D positions (SYM-FF/SYM-GRU) had the lowest cross-validation accuracy but generalized best to held-out players and checkpoints (0.850 identity and human-agent accuracy). Visual models (VIS-FF 0.633) overfit despite being closest to what human judges see. All classifiers fail at finer-grained agent-vs-agent judgments: hybrid-symbolic accuracy is at most 0.525 and all rank correlations are negative. This holds even though humans consistently judge the hybrid (depth-seeing) agent more human-like (0.78 / 0.62 of judges). Human judgments also appear context-dependent: certainty and preferences differed significantly between the two studies, possibly from anchoring or exposure effects.
method: Problem setup: binary classification of trajectories x_{0:T} as human vs agent, trained with BCE on proxy labels from the known source; human judgments are used only at test time; evaluation uses accuracy vs majority vote and Spearman rank correlation vs the fraction of judges.

Input spaces: SYM (absolute 3D agent position per step); VIS (320x200 game frames without overlays); TD (one top-down 2D image of the whole trajectory, projecting position along z); BC (bar-code: each frame averaged along y into one line, lines stacked, e.g. 320x600 for 600 frames).

Six classifiers: SYM-FF and SYM-GRU (MLP/GRU trained from scratch); VIS-FF (ImageNet VGG-16 per frame); VIS-GRU (VGG-16 + GRU); TD-CNN and BC-CNN (VGG-16 on single images). The VGG last layer is replaced by a 1-2 layer FF head with dropout. Hyperparameters (dropout, hidden size, sequence length 5/10/20) are tuned by 5-fold CV. SYM-FF and VIS-FF mirror GAIL-style discriminators.

Trajectory aggregation: sub-sequence models classify every non-overlapping sub-sequence and pick the video with the higher percentage of 'human' predictions (majority vote). Whole-trajectory models (TD/BC) pick the higher human likelihood.

Navigation agents (data generators, following Alonso et al. 2020): PPO, trained on 60 parallel game instances with domain-randomized spawns over 26 locations. Two variants: a symbolic agent (goal relative angle/distance, position, average frame depth; MLP) and a hybrid agent (the same plus a 32x32 depth buffer through a CNN). Both use 8 discrete actions and a reward of dense distance-to-goal, +1 goal, -1 death, -0.01 per step; episodes last at most 3,000 ticks.

Human NTT: two IRB-approved online studies with 60 participants (30 each). Each study has 10 side-by-side video trials (6 human-vs-agent, 4 hybrid-vs-symbolic) matched on goal location. Participants answer a 2AFC 'Which video is more likely to be human?', give a free-text rationale, and rate certainty on a 5-point Likert scale.

Data protocol: 100 human episodes (4 players) plus 198 agent episodes (2 checkpoints) for training and validation. The test set is 40 HNTT videos from 3 different players and a different agent checkpoint, so there is no overlap. Results are mean (std) over 5 training repeats.

setting.backbone: ANTT classifiers: feedforward / GRU on 3D positions (trained from scratch), ImageNet-pretrained VGG-16 (+GRU) on frames / top-down / bar-code images (fine-tuned head). Navigation agents: PPO MLP (symbolic) and CNN+MLP (hybrid) policies trained from scratch
setting.training_data: Classifiers: 100 human navigation episodes (4 players) + 198 agent episodes (2 PPO checkpoints), proxy human/agent labels, 5-fold CV; human judgments (60 participants) only for test evaluation on 40 held-out videos. Agents: PPO in the game, 20M training steps
setting.observation: Classifier: agent 3D positions or 320x200 game video frames (or compressed top-down / bar-code images). Agents: goal relative angle/distance + position + average depth (symbolic), plus a 32x32 depth buffer (hybrid)
setting.action_space: Agents: 8 discrete actions (none, forward, left/right by 30/45/90 degrees); classifier outputs binary human/agent
setting.simulator: other: proprietary modern AAA 3D video game by Ninja Theory (~500x320 m map, 16 goal locations)
setting.privileged: none for classifiers; navigation agents observe the relative goal angle/distance and absolute position from game state

numbers_note: This is not a standard navigation benchmark. Results are classifier agreement with ground-truth identity and human judgments on a custom 40-video held-out test set in a proprietary game. Accuracies printed as fractions (e.g., 0.850) are converted to 0-100; Spearman ranks are kept as printed. Two further variants in Table 4 are omitted: VIS-FF (0.633 / 0.633 / −0.041 / 0.225 / −0.165) and BC-CNN (0.717 / 0.717 / −0.009 / 0.475 / −0.095). Human-judge (HNTT) statistics are given in the text and figures only: detection 0.84 in Study 1 and 0.77 in Study 2; hybrid preferred by 0.78 and 0.62 of judges. PPO agent task performance is shown only in a figure (time-to-goal curves).
results: Human judges identified real human players above chance: mean 0.84 in Study 1 and 0.77 in Study 2. They also preferred the hybrid depth-seeing agent over the symbolic one (0.78 and 0.62 of judges), showing that high task success does not imply human-likeness. The symbolic classifiers SYM-FF and SYM-GRU match human judges best on human-vs-agent pairs, with 0.850 accuracy; SYM-FF has the best rank correlation (0.364). They beat the visual GAIL-style discriminator VIS-FF (0.633) and TD-CNN (0.583). No classifier captures human preferences between the two agents: hybrid-symbolic accuracy is 0.225–0.525 and all rank correlations are negative.
limitations: Very small data: 140 human recordings from 7 players, 10 test trials per study, and 40 test videos. The evaluation is in a single proprietary game map, restricted to ground-based navigation with flying and jumping excluded.
The classifiers cannot capture fine-grained human-likeness differences between agents; hybrid-symbolic accuracy is near or below chance and rank correlations are negative.

The authors explicitly advise against using the classifiers as rewards, since agents can exploit static discriminators. Human judgments also appear context-dependent (possible anchoring effects between studies).
